claims.claim: Across 13 studies, nearly 4 in 10 adults at routine medical visits were accompanied, usually by a spouse or an adult child; accompanied patients were older and in worse health.
claims.supporting_passage: The weighted mean rate of patient accompaniment to routine adult medical visits was 37.6% in 13 contributing studies. Accompanied patients were significantly older and more likely to be female, less educated, and in worse physical and mental health than unaccompanied patients. Companions were on average 63 years of age, predominantly female (79.4%), and spouses (54.7%) or adult children (32.2%) of patients.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults at routine physician visits (13 studies) / accompanied by a family companion / unaccompanied / rate and characteristics / single visits
claims.safe_wording: Across 13 studies, nearly 4 in 10 adults at routine medical appointments brought someone with them, most often a husband, wife or grown-up child. The people who brought someone were, on average, older and in poorer health.
claims.qualifications: Say 'routine medical appointments'; the figure is a weighted average across studies, not a UK figure. Do not describe the companions as mainly daughters: the review reports spouses 54.7% and adult children 32.2%.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The review is from 2011; accompaniment rates may differ now and by country. Country mix of the 13 studies not confirmed from the abstract.

numbers.meaning: weighted mean rate of accompaniment to routine adult medical visits, 13 studies; 'nearly 4 in 10'
share of companions who were spouses and adult children respectively
average age of companions in years

claims.claim: In videotaped US geriatric primary care visits with 93 patients, those whose companions asked them questions, prompted them to talk and asked their opinion were more likely to be active in decision-making (cross-sectional association).
claims.supporting_passage: Patients (N = 93) in this cross-sectional sample range in age from 65 to 95 years and are mostly white (n = 73, 79%) and female (n = 67, 72%). ... Patients whose companions facilitated their involvement in the medical visit by asking the patient questions, prompting the patient to talk, and asking for the patient's opinion were more than four times as likely to be active in decision-making as patients whose companions did not assist in this manner (unadjusted OR 3.5, CI 1.4-8.7, p < .01; adjusted OR 4.5, CI 1.6-12.4, p < .01).
claims.pico_timeframe: 93 accompanied patients aged 65 to 95, US geriatric primary care / companion facilitates patient involvement (asks patient questions, prompts talk, asks opinion) / companions who did not / patient active in decision-making during the visit / single visit, cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In a US study that filmed 93 GP visits by people aged 65 to 95 who came with a relative or friend, patients were more likely to take an active part in decisions when the companion asked them questions, prompted them to speak and asked what they thought. The study looked at one visit each, so it shows a link, not proof that the companion's behaviour caused the difference.
claims.qualifications: Association only (cross-sectional). Do not write 'four times as likely' or any multiplier: the figure is an odds ratio (adjusted OR 4.5, 95% CI 1.6 to 12.4) with a wide interval. Say 'more likely'. Small, mostly white, mostly female US sample. Sicker patients' companions were more likely to facilitate, so the groups differed.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Reverse direction is possible: patients who wish to be active may draw their companions into prompting them. No trial tests coaching companions to do this.

numbers.meaning: patients aged 65 to 95 in the study
odds of active patient decision-making with vs without companion facilitation; practitioner posts only, as an odds ratio; never 'times more likely'

claims.claim: When a third person was present, older patients raised fewer topics, were less assertive, and were frequently excluded from the conversation (small US matched comparison).
claims.supporting_passage: In a sample of 96 audiotaped initial medical visits, 15 encounters involved three persons. These 15 cases were matched with 15 dyadic interviews for gender and race of the patient and for gender and race of the physician. ... The specific content and the quality of interactional processes of physicians were not affected by the presence of a third person. However, older patients raised fewer topics in all content areas (medical, personal habits, psychosocial, and physician-patient relationship) in triads than in dyads. ... Patients were rated as less assertive and expressive, and there was less joint decision-making and shared laughter in triads than in dyads. Patients were frequently excluded from conversations in visits in which a third person was present.
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients aged 60 and over at a first visit to hospital-based primary care physicians, US / third person present (15 visits) / matched visits without (15) / patient topics raised, assertiveness, joint decision-making, exclusion / single audiotaped visit
claims.safe_wording: In a small US study that compared 15 first appointments where an older patient came with someone against 15 where they came alone, patients who were accompanied raised fewer topics themselves and were often left out of the conversation.
claims.qualifications: Small (15 vs 15), 1994, US, audiotaped first visits only. It does not show that doctors 'turn to the companion': the authors found the doctors' content and interaction quality were not affected; the change was in the patient's participation and exclusion from conversations. Use 'often left out of the conversation', not 'doctors talk to the relative instead'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Wolff and Roter 2011 found accompanied patients plus companions contributed about as much talk as unaccompanied patients, and Clayman 2005 found companions did more enabling than detracting things, so exclusion is not universal.

numbers.meaning: matched three-person and two-person visits, out of 96 recorded

claims.claim: Some companion behaviours (informational support) are seen as helpful and others (dominating or demanding) as less helpful; preferences vary, and agreeing roles is a proposed strategy.
claims.supporting_passage: Of the 8409 titles identified, 52 studies were included. ... Results indicated companions regularly attended consultations, were frequently perceived as helpful, and assumed a variety of roles. However, their involvement often raised challenges. Patients with increased need were more often accompanied. Some companion behaviours were felt to be more helpful (e.g. informational support) and less helpful (e.g. dominating/demanding behaviours), and preferences for involvement varied widely. ... Preliminary strategies for health professionals include (i) encourage/involve companions, (ii) highlight helpful companion behaviours, (iii) clarify and agree upon role preferences of patient/companions.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult patients with adult companions in medical consultations (52 studies) / companion behaviours and roles / not applicable / perceived helpfulness, role preferences / cross-sectional and qualitative
claims.safe_wording: A review of 52 studies found that companions were often seen as helpful, but taking over or making demands was seen as less helpful, and people differed widely in how much they wanted a companion to do. That is why it helps to agree beforehand what your parent wants to say themselves and what they want you to add.
claims.qualifications: The 'agree beforehand' step is practical advice consistent with the review's proposed strategy for professionals (clarify and agree role preferences); it has not been tested as a family intervention. Present it as advice, not as a finding.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Strategies are described by the authors as preliminary.

numbers.meaning: studies in the systematic review

claims.claim: Companions showed autonomy-detracting behaviours (controlling the patient, building alliances with the doctor), and these go with less patient involvement.
claims.supporting_passage: These behaviors were coded throughout the visit using an autonomy-based framework that included both autonomy enhancing (i.e. facilitating patient understanding, patient involvement, and doctor understanding) and detracting behaviors, (i.e. controlling the patient and building alliances with the physician). ... Companions are active participants in medical visits and engage in more autonomy enhancing than detracting behaviors.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C09-09-b
claims.safe_wording: In the same study, companions did more to help the patient take part than to take over.
claims.qualifications: The abstract confirms that controlling and alliance-building behaviours were coded and were less common than enabling behaviours. It does not report that they were linked with less patient involvement, so the candidate's clause 'controlling or siding with the doctor goes with less [involvement]' must be dropped.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Full text not available in this project to check the detracting-behaviour analysis.

claims.claim: When a companion was present, clinicians gave more biomedical information; effects of accompaniment on patient outcomes were inconclusive or favourable.
claims.supporting_passage: Accompanied patient visits were significantly longer, but verbal contribution to medical dialog was comparable when accompanied patients and their family companion were compared with unaccompanied patients. When a companion was present, health care providers engaged in more biomedical information giving. Given the diversity of outcomes, pooled estimates could not be calculated: of 5 contributing studies 0 were unfavorable, 3 inconclusive, and 2 favorable for accompanied relative to unaccompanied patients.
claims.pico_timeframe: Routine adult physician visits / companion present / companion absent / visit length, talk, information giving, patient outcomes (5 studies) / single visits
claims.safe_wording: When someone came with the patient, appointments were longer and doctors gave more medical information. None of five studies found worse outcomes for patients who were accompanied.
claims.qualifications: Only 5 studies on outcomes; 3 inconclusive. Do not claim companions improve outcomes.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: None beyond the small number of outcome studies.

numbers.meaning: outcome studies unfavourable, inconclusive and favourable for accompanied patients

claims.claim: In a 2026 systematic review of 18 RCTs (1985 participants), there was no clear pattern of effect of teach-back on patient knowledge (very low certainty); the 9 knowledge trials could not be pooled.
claims.supporting_passage: Our systematic review included 18 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1985 participants. Across 9 RCTs assessing knowledge acquisition, conceptual inconsistencies precluded meta-analysis. Overall, there was no clear pattern of the effect of teach-back on knowledge (very low COE). ... In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we did not identify a clear benefit of teach-back on knowledge acquisition
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult patients and/or care partners / teach-back in a single encounter / comparator (usually usual care) / knowledge acquisition / proximal outcomes, short term
claims.safe_wording: A 2026 review of 18 randomised trials, with about 2,000 people, found no clear effect of teach-back on what patients knew afterwards. The evidence was rated very low certainty, and the 9 trials that measured knowledge were too different to combine.
claims.qualifications: This is an evidence gap, not evidence that teach-back fails: say 'has not been shown' or 'no clear effect', never 'does not work'. The review covered teach-back in a single encounter only; multi-session education programmes that include teach-back were outside its scope. The trials were in adults generally, not older people specifically.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Talevski 2020 (20 studies of mixed design and quality) reported teach-back effective in 19 of 20 studies, including knowledge outcomes. The difference probably reflects Vick's RCT-only, single-encounter criteria and GRADE rating; state that the newer, stricter review is less certain than earlier ones.

numbers.meaning: randomised controlled trials in the review
participants across the 18 trials ('about 2,000')
trials that measured knowledge; not pooled

claims.claim: Teach-back increased self-efficacy (5 RCTs, very low certainty) and self-reported short-term adherence (7 RCTs, low certainty), with wide confidence intervals and substantial heterogeneity.
claims.supporting_passage: In a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs assessing self-efficacy (416 participants), we found that teach-back interventions led to a large increase in self-efficacy relative to usual care (SMD = 2.40; 95%CI 0.37-4.44) (very low COE). In a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs assessing adherence to health behaviors (571 participants), teach-back interventions led to a large increase in adherence (SMD = 1.04; 95%CI 0.45-1.64) (low COE). Meta-analyses for both self-efficacy and adherence had large confidence intervals that ranged from small to large effect sizes and had substantial heterogeneity. ... but did find evidence that teach-back improves self-efficacy and self-reported, short-term adherence to health behaviors.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adult patients and/or care partners / single-encounter teach-back / usual care / self-efficacy; self-reported adherence to health behaviours / short term
claims.safe_wording: Teach-back did improve patients' confidence in managing their health and their own reports of sticking to advice in the short term, but the certainty was low or very low and the size of the effect was very uncertain.
claims.qualifications: Say 'self-reported' and 'short term' for adherence. Do not present standardised mean differences to the public; for practitioners give them only with the certainty rating. Do not describe the effects as 'large' without the certainty caveat.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Wide confidence intervals (self-efficacy 0.37 to 4.44; adherence 0.45 to 1.64) and substantial heterogeneity.

numbers.meaning: self-efficacy meta-analysis; SMD 2.40 (95% CI 0.37 to 4.44); very low certainty
adherence meta-analysis; SMD 1.04 (95% CI 0.45 to 1.64); low certainty; self-reported, short term

claims.claim: Teach-back is widely presented as an effective, high-quality communication strategy.
claims.supporting_passage: Vick 2026: "Teach-back has been identified as a high-quality clinical communication strategy." Talevski 2020: "Use of 'teach-back' has been shown to improve patients' knowledge and self-care abilities, however there is little guidance for healthcare services seeking to embed teach-back in their setting." ... "Overall, 20 studies of moderate quality were included in this review (four rated high, nine rated moderate, seven rated weak)." ... "Use of teach-back proved effective in 19 of the 20 studies, ranging from learning-related outcomes (e.g. knowledge recall and retention) to objective health-related outcomes (e.g. hospital re-admissions, quality of life)."
claims.pico_timeframe: Description of how teach-back is presented in the literature; Talevski: 20 studies of mixed design to July 2019
claims.safe_wording: Teach-back is often taught as a proven way to improve understanding: an earlier review reported it worked in 19 of 20 studies. The newer review, which included only randomised trials and graded their certainty, is much less sure about knowledge.
claims.qualifications: The NHS or Health Education England guidance recommending teach-back could not be identified or opened, so do not name any NHS body as recommending it. 'Often taught as proven' is supported only as a description of the literature.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The two reviews differ in inclusion criteria (Talevski included non-randomised studies and teach-back within structured education; Vick only RCTs of single-encounter teach-back).

numbers.meaning: studies in Talevski 2020 reporting teach-back effective on some outcome (mixed designs, 7 rated weak)

claims.claim: Older patients remember less than younger patients when more information is given in a consultation.
claims.supporting_passage: Recall decreased significantly with age, but only when total amount of information presented was taken into account. This indicates that if more information is discussed, older patients have more trouble remembering the information than younger ones. ... Recall is not simply a function of patient age. Age only predicts recall when controlling for amount of information presented. Both prognosis and information about prognosis are better predictors of recall than age.
claims.pico_timeframe: 260 patients with cancer at a first oncology consultation / age, amount of information given / younger patients / recall measured by structured telephone interview against audio recordings / shortly after consultation
claims.safe_wording: In a study that checked what 260 people with cancer remembered against recordings of their first oncology appointment, older patients recalled less than younger ones when a lot of information was given. Age alone was a weaker guide than how much was said, and how serious the news was.
claims.qualifications: Oncology only; the age effect depends on the amount of information. Do not say 'older people forget most of what they are told'. This replaces the candidate's Kessels 2003 claim (see C09-23-f).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Prognosis and information about prognosis predicted recall better than age.

numbers.meaning: patients with cancer in the recall study

claims.claim: Teach-back is recommended in NHS health literacy guidance.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not name any NHS document or body as recommending teach-back.
claims.qualifications: No NHS, NHS England or Health Education England document was identified or opened in this project.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not searched further to conserve usage; the post does not need it (C09-23-c covers 'widely taught').

claims.claim: Patients forget a large share of medical information soon after a consultation, and older age is associated with poorer recall (Kessels 2003).
claims.location: Not found: PubMed record PMID 12724430 has no abstract, and the PMC record PMC539473 returned no text
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Do not quote a percentage of information forgotten. Use C09-23-d (Jansen 2008) for the older-patient point.
claims.qualifications: Kessels 2003 is a narrative review whose often-quoted figures come from older studies; the text could not be read here.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable

claims.claim: The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges 2018 guidance 'Please, write to me' recommends that outpatient clinic letters be written directly to patients.
claims.supporting_passage: Ong 2026 (full text, Introduction): "Key drivers for this shift include the 2018 Academy of Medical Royal Colleges (AoMRC) guidance, ‘Please, write to me’, which established the best practice of writing letters directly to patients rather than about them." Lonergan 2019 (abstract): "Recent guidelines from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges recommend that all OPD letters should be written directly to the patient." Gupta 2021 (abstract): "The Academy of Medical Royal Colleges have recently recommended all outpatient letters to be written directly to patients." Search extract (not opened): the guidance "aims to encourage doctors to write most of their outpatient clinic letters directly to patients and send a copy to the patient's General Practitioner".
claims.location: Ong 2026 Introduction and Discussion; Lonergan 2019 and Gupta 2021 abstracts; AoMRC web page search extract
claims.pico_timeframe: UK hospital doctors writing outpatient clinic letters / guidance from 2018
claims.safe_wording: National guidance from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges (2018) recommends that hospital doctors write outpatient clinic letters to the patient, rather than about the patient to the GP. If your letters are written to your GP, you can ask whether future letters could be written to you.
claims.qualifications: Follow the editor: say 'national guidance recommends', never 'entitled to' or 'your right'. It is professional guidance, not law. Avoid 'all' and 'most' (secondary sources disagree on which word the guidance uses). The primary document was not opened; three peer-reviewed papers describe the recommendation consistently. The 'copy to the GP' detail rests on a search extract only, so leave it out or keep it general.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Uptake is low: Ong 2026 describes a 'persistent gap between policy recommendations and real-world practice'.

numbers.meaning: year of the AoMRC guidance

claims.claim: Of 4.6 million outpatient letters at Moorfields Eye Hospital (2013 to 2025), about 2 in 100 were classified as addressed to patients and about 95 in 100 were less readable than recommended.
claims.supporting_passage: The dataset comprised 4 648 289 letters from 804 986 patients (median 3, IQR 1–6 letters per patient) over the 13 year study period. ... age of 53 (IQR 31–69) years at the baseline visit. ... FRE had a median value of 51.1 (IQR 41.9–58.5), indicating substantially lower readability than the suggested reference range of 70–90 for patient-facing materials. ... Overall, 95.3% of letters fell below the recommended FRE range ... Only a minority of letters (2.25%) were classified as patient-addressed. There was a small annual increase in the likelihood of letters being addressed directly to patients over time ... Based on this exploratory review, a pragmatic threshold of at least six second-person pronouns per 100 words was selected to classify letters as patient addressed for subsequent analyses.
claims.pico_timeframe: All outpatient clinic letters, Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust (London), 17 subspecialties, 1 Jan 2013 to 1 Nov 2025 / letter text / recommended Flesch Reading Ease range 70 to 90 / readability and patient-addressed classification
claims.safe_wording: At one large London eye hospital, researchers analysed 4.6 million clinic letters written between 2013 and 2025. About 2 in 100 were written to the patient. About 95 in 100 were harder to read than the level recommended for patients.
claims.qualifications: Always name it as one eye hospital; do not generalise to all clinics or all of the NHS. 'Written to the patient' was judged by a computer rule (at least 6 uses of 'you' or 'your' per 100 words), which the authors call imperfect. Patients were all ages (median 53), not an older-age sample. The study measured reading level, not whether patients understood.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The share addressed to patients rose slightly each year, from a low base.

numbers.meaning: clinic letters analysed, 2013 to 2025, one eye hospital
letters classified as written to the patient; 'about 2 in 100'
letters below the recommended Flesch Reading Ease range of 70 to 90; 'about 95 in 100'
median Flesch Reading Ease score (recommended 70 to 90); practitioner posts only

claims.claim: In the NHS, patients often receive a copy of the clinic letter even when it is addressed to the GP.
claims.supporting_passage: The practice of sending copies of clinical letters directly to patients is well established in the National Health Service (NHS) in the United Kingdom (UK), where these letters serve several key purposes simultaneously ... Letters could be addressed to—and therefore written for—healthcare professionals or patients and copied to the other party.
claims.pico_timeframe: UK NHS outpatient correspondence (background statement)
claims.safe_wording: Many people already get a copy of the clinic letter, but it is usually written to the GP and about them.
claims.qualifications: Background statement from a paper's introduction, not a measured finding; do not give a figure for how many people receive copies. Rephrase the candidate angle: do not say the letter is 'the only lasting record most older people get' (unsupported).
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: No data on how often older patients receive copies.

claims.claim: In a urology quality improvement project, most patients interviewed after receiving a restructured clinic letter found it easy to understand and said it improved their understanding.
claims.supporting_passage: In one OPD, 71% of patients stated that they wished to receive a copy of their letter. ... Following the implementation of the intervention, letters were sent to 120 patients and feedback was obtained from 63 patients with either a feedback postcard or telephone interview. Of the 53 patients who agreed to participate in the telephone feedback, 39 (74%) found the letter easy to understand, 49 (92%) reported it was accurate and summarised the consultation as they remembered it and 38 (72%) reported that reading the letter improved their understanding of their OPD visit. All patients said they would like to receive similar letters from future OPD consultations.
claims.pico_timeframe: Urology outpatients, Tallaght University Hospital, Dublin / restructured clinic letter sent to patient / no comparator / self-reported understanding and accuracy / after a 90-day improvement cycle
claims.safe_wording: In one Dublin urology clinic that redesigned its letters and sent them to patients, 39 of the 53 patients interviewed found the letter easy to understand, and 38 said it helped them understand their visit.
claims.qualifications: Irish, not UK. Small, uncontrolled, self-reported; only 53 of 120 recipients gave telephone feedback. The abstract does not say the letters were addressed to the patient, so say 'sent to patients' rather than 'written to them'.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Responder bias likely.

numbers.meaning: telephone respondents who found the letter easy to understand
said reading the letter improved understanding of their visit
patients sent letters; 63 gave any feedback
patients in one clinic who wanted a copy of their letter (baseline survey; denominator not given in abstract)

claims.claim: In a UK head and neck clinic survey, about half of patients preferred letters written to them and very few preferred letters to the GP, yet all sampled surgeon letters were addressed to GPs.
claims.supporting_passage: Of all 80 included patient responses, 42 expressed a preference for letters to be written directly to the patient (52.5%). Only 5.0% (n = 4) of respondents exhibited a preference for letters to be written to their GP, with 42.5% (n = 34) of patients having no preference. All 54 surgeon letters (100%) were addressed to GPs.
claims.pico_timeframe: 80 patients at one English head and neck outpatient department / questionnaire on preferred letter style / 2 weeks; 54 surgeon letters sampled retrospectively
claims.safe_wording: In a survey at one English hospital clinic, 42 of 80 patients wanted letters written to them, 4 wanted them written to their GP and the rest had no preference. Every one of the 54 surgeons' letters checked was written to the GP.
claims.qualifications: One clinic, small sample, not an older-age sample.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: A large share (34 of 80) had no preference, so do not say 'most patients want letters written to them'.

numbers.meaning: preferred letters written to the patient
preferred letters written to the GP
no preference
sampled surgeon letters addressed to GPs

claims.claim: Patients who need a different format (large print, easy read) can ask for it under the Accessible Information Standard (England) or as a reasonable adjustment under the Equality Act 2010; and patients can say if they would rather letters were not sent to their home.
claims.location: Not found. A web search returned only a law firm's summary for the home-delivery point, which is not an official source and was not opened.
claims.pico_timeframe: Not applicable
claims.safe_wording: Leave both points out of the post, including the judge's suggested line about letters not coming to the home, unless a later batch opens the Accessible Information Standard or the AoMRC guidance itself.
claims.qualifications: Official web pages could not be opened; no copy was found in Drive.

claims.claim: In 16 studies with 2595 patient-surrogate pairs answering hypothetical scenarios, surrogates predicted patients' treatment preferences with 68% accuracy.
claims.supporting_passage: The search identified 16 eligible studies, involving 151 hypothetical scenarios and 2595 surrogate-patient pairs, which collectively analyzed 19 526 patient-surrogate paired responses. Overall, surrogates predicted patients' treatment preferences with 68% accuracy. ... Patient-designated and next-of-kin surrogates incorrectly predict patients' end-of-life treatment preferences in one third of cases.
claims.pico_timeframe: Patients and their patient-designated or next-of-kin surrogates / surrogate predicts patient's answer / patient's own answer / agreement on hypothetical end-of-life treatment scenarios / single time point
claims.safe_wording: When researchers asked people and the relative who would speak for them the same questions about treatment near the end of life, the relatives gave the same answer as the person about 2 times in 3, and a different answer about 1 time in 3. These were imagined situations, not real decisions.
claims.qualifications: Hypothetical end-of-life scenarios, not real decisions. 68% is across answers (19,526 paired responses), not the proportion of relatives who were 'right' overall. Do not say 'mostly US' (not verified from the abstract). The review is from 2006.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Some agreement is expected by chance on yes/no questions, so 68% is not directly comparable with zero. Later structured-planning trials improved agreement (C09-25-d).

numbers.meaning: accuracy of surrogates' predictions across 19,526 paired responses; 'about 2 in 3'
share of predictions that were wrong; 'about 1 in 3'
size of the evidence base

claims.claim: Neither the patient choosing the surrogate nor prior discussion of preferences improved surrogates' accuracy.
claims.supporting_passage: Neither patient designation of surrogates nor prior discussion of patients' treatment preferences improved surrogates' predictive accuracy.
claims.pico_timeframe: As C09-25-a; comparison of surrogates chosen by the patient vs next of kin, and pairs who had vs had not discussed preferences (observational comparisons within the included studies)
claims.safe_wording: In those studies, relatives the person had chosen were no more accurate than next of kin, and couples or families who said they had talked about it beforehand were no more accurate than those who had not.
claims.qualifications: This applies to ordinary, unstructured prior discussion in the observational studies reviewed. It must not be presented as 'talking does not help'. Pair it with C09-25-d. The judge's values note applies: keep encouraging conversations alongside writing things down.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Kirchhoff 2010 (RCT) found that a structured, facilitated planning interview greatly improved surrogate understanding.

claims.claim: The studies used hypothetical end-of-life scenarios, mostly in the US.
claims.supporting_passage: The search identified 16 eligible studies, involving 151 hypothetical scenarios and 2595 surrogate-patient pairs
claims.pico_timeframe: As C09-25-a
claims.safe_wording: The studies used imagined end-of-life situations rather than real decisions.
claims.qualifications: 'Hypothetical' is confirmed; 'mostly in the US' is not verified (full text not accessible), so leave the country out.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Not applicable

claims.claim: A structured, facilitated planning conversation improved surrogates' understanding of patients' goals in a randomised trial; reviews of joint patient-family planning suggest it may improve agreement.
claims.supporting_passage: Kirchhoff 2010: "Trained health professionals conducted a structured, patient-centered interview intended to promote informed decision-making and to result in the completion of a document clarifying the goals of the patient with regard to four disease-specific health outcome situations and the degree of decision-making latitude granted to the surrogate. ... Three hundred thirteen patient-surrogate pairs completed the study. As measured according to kappa scores and in all four situations and in the degree of latitude, intervention group surrogates demonstrated a significantly higher degree of understanding of patient goals than control group surrogates. Intervention group kappa scores ranged from 0.61 to 0.78, whereas control group kappa scores ranged from 0.07 to 0.28." Liu 2024: "In total, 14 randomized controlled trials were included. ... In addition, interventions may improve dyad's congruence on end-of-life care, family caregivers' confidence in surrogate decision-making, and quality of end-of-life communication."
claims.pico_timeframe: Kirchhoff: competent adults with chronic heart failure or chronic kidney disease and their surrogates, six Wisconsin clinics, 2004 to 2007 / facilitated disease-specific planning interview with a written document / usual care / surrogate understanding of patient goals (kappa agreement) / timing not stated in abstract. Liu: 14 RCTs of patient-caregiver advance care planning / usual care / congruence (narrative), documentation (pooled)
claims.safe_wording: Talking in a structured way can help. In a US trial with 313 people with heart or kidney disease and the relatives who would speak for them, a planning conversation led by a trained professional, which ended in a written record of the person's goals, left relatives with a much better understanding of those goals than usual care.
claims.qualifications: One US trial in adults with heart failure or kidney disease; facilitated by trained staff, with a written document. For the public describe the agreement as 'much better understanding'; do not quote kappa values to the public. Liu 2024's congruence finding is narrative ('may improve'), not pooled.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Liu 2024 notes the need for further studies; the companion trial (Kirchhoff 2012) (PMID 22458336, abstract read) found fewer unmet resuscitation wishes with planning (1 of 62 vs 6 of 48) but the difference was not statistically significant; not needed for this post, so not listed as a source.

numbers.meaning: patient-surrogate pairs completing the Kirchhoff trial
agreement between surrogate and patient goals, intervention vs control; practitioner posts only, with a plain reading (good vs slight agreement)
RCTs in Liu 2024 review

candidates.reason: The core insight is supported. Wolff and Roter 2011 gives the accompaniment rate (37.6%, 13 studies; mostly spouses and adult children). Clayman 2005 gives the link between prompting the patient and the patient's active decision-making (cross-sectional; say 'more likely', no multiplier). Greene 1994 supports 'older patients were often left out of the conversation' when a third person was present (small US study); it does not support 'clinicians turn to the companion', which the writer must not say. Laidsaar-Powell 2013 supports the before-the-appointment step as advice (agree roles; dominating behaviour seen as less helpful). Drop the angle clause that controlling or siding with the doctor 'goes with less' involvement: the abstract does not report that association (C09-09-e).

Vick 2026 (18 RCTs, 1985 participants) confirms, word for word, no clear pattern of effect on knowledge (very low certainty, not pooled) and increases in self-efficacy (very low) and self-reported short-term adherence (low), with wide CIs and heterogeneity. Present it as 'not shown', never 'does not work', and note the review's scope: single-encounter teach-back in adults, not older people specifically. 'Often taught as proven' is supported by Vick's background and by the more favourable Talevski 2020 review (19 of 20 mixed-design studies), which the post should name as the contrasting earlier evidence. The NHS guidance claim was not found; drop it. Kessels 2003 could not be read; replace it with Jansen 2008 for the older-patient angle (older patients recall less when more information is given). Using teach-back to check your own explanation is professional judgement and must be worded as such.

The AoMRC 2018 recommendation is supported by three peer-reviewed descriptions (Ong 2026 full text; Lonergan 2019 and Gupta 2021 abstracts); the guidance itself could not be opened. Wording must follow the editor ('national guidance recommends', not 'entitled'), and should avoid 'all' or 'most'. Ong 2026 figures are confirmed in full text: 2.25% patient-addressed and 95.3% below recommended readability, at one London eye hospital, using a rule-based proxy, patients of all ages (median 53). Changes needed: (1) the angle claim that the letter is 'the only lasting record most older people get' is unsupported, and Ong notes that copies to patients are well established in the NHS; (2) the Accessible Information Standard / Equality Act claim and the judge's 'letters not sent to your home' line were not verified, so both must be omitted; (3) Lonergan is Irish, and its abstract says letters were 'sent to' patients, not written to them.
candidates.revised_angle: Many people get a copy of their hospital clinic letter, but it is usually written to the GP and about them. National guidance from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges (2018) recommends that doctors write clinic letters to the patient. In one large London eye hospital, about 2 in 100 of 4.6 million letters were written to the patient, and about 95 in 100 were harder to read than recommended. In a survey at one English clinic, about half of patients wanted letters written to them; only 4 of 80 preferred letters to the GP. Ask this: 'Could you write the letter to me, please?'

candidates.reason: Shalowitz 2006 confirms, word for word, 68% accuracy (16 studies, 2595 pairs, hypothetical end-of-life scenarios) and that neither designation nor prior discussion improved accuracy. However, 'even after a conversation' holds only for informal discussion in the observational comparisons reviewed. Kirchhoff 2010 (RCT, 313 pairs) found a structured, facilitated planning interview with a written record greatly improved surrogates' understanding, and Liu 2024 (14 RCTs) suggests joint planning may improve agreement. The message must become 'talk it through in a structured way and write it down', which also meets the judge's values concern. 'Mostly US' could not be verified; omit it.
candidates.revised_angle: When relatives were asked to predict a person's answers to imagined end-of-life treatment questions, they matched about 2 times in 3 (Shalowitz 2006). Being chosen by the person, or having chatted about it, did not make them more accurate in those studies. In a US trial, a structured planning conversation with a trained professional, ending in a written record of the person's goals, left relatives understanding those goals much better. So record your own views and reasons while you can, and go through them with the person who would speak for you, ideally with a professional's help. Clinicians should ask relatives what the person valued and said, not only what they would choose.
